query: What are the regulations for SCBA packs on my vessel?

haiku.answer:
**For your US-flagged 30,000 GT tanker operating on coastal routes, self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) requirements are set by 46 CFR Subchapter D (tank vessels), implemented via SOLAS Ch.II-2 Reg.10, and enforced by ABS class survey.**

---

## BINDING REQUIREMENT — SCBA QUANTITY & SPECS

**46 CFR 34.05** (Fire-fighter's outfits) requires you to carry fire-fighter's outfits on board. For a tank vessel of your size, the quantity is determined by cargo volume and vessel type, governed by SOLAS Ch.II-2 Reg.10.2 and your ABS class rules (ABS MVR Pt.4 Ch.7 Sec.3).

**Each SCBA pack must meet these specifications:**

| Requirement | Spec |
|---|---|
| **Breathing apparatus type** | Self-contained compressed air-operated, pressure-demand, open-circuit type |
| **Air cylinder volume** | Minimum 1,200 liters (or capable of functioning ≥30 min) |
| **Audible/visual alarm** | Yes — must alert user before air drops below 200 liters |
| **Lifeline** | Fireproof, ≥30 m length, rated for 3.5 kN static load over 5 min, snap-hook attachment |
| **Personal protective equipment** | Heat-resistant protective clothing (water-resistant outer surface), rubber/non-conducting boots, rigid helmet, explosion-proof electric safety lamp (≥3 hr burn), insulated axe |
| **Air cylinder interchangeability** | All cylinders must be interchangeable across all SCBA aboard |

Per USCG MSM 16000.72 Ch.2, approved SCBA must be certified by NIOSH and MSHA. Fresh-air apparatus (pre-1992 models) may not be used as replacements.

---

## SPARE CHARGES & AIR SUPPLY

**Two spare air charges per SCBA** are required *unless* your vessel is equipped with a suitably located, contamination-free air recharging means (SOLAS Ch.II-2 Reg.10.2.5). If you have such a compressor or high-pressure storage system, you may carry only one spare charge per apparatus.

**Recharging equipment options** (if carried):
- Breathing air compressor: ≥60 L/min per required SCBA, max 420 L/min total; supplied from main or emergency switchboard, or independently driven
- High-pressure storage system: ≥1,200 L per required SCBA, up to 50,000 L total free air capacity

All spare air cylinders must be hydrostatically tested every 5 years (per OCIMF SIRE guidance); test date must be stamped on the cylinder. Drop-in pressure when charged and valve closed must not exceed 10 bars per minute (manufacturer inspection standard).

---

## STORAGE LOCATION

**SOLAS Ch.II-2 Reg.10.3.1** requires fire-fighter's outfits to be stored in an easily accessible, permanently marked location. For tankers, SOLAS allows storage in widely separated positions — this supports rescue operations if one area is inaccessible due to fire or damage.

---

## ABS CLASS ADDITIONS

Your ABS-classed vessel is also subject to **ABS MVR Pt.4 Ch.7 Sec.3** fire-safety requirements, which parallel SOLAS but add class-survey inspection detail. ABS requires two spare charges per apparatus (unless you have a dedicated recharging compressor), and all SCBA must pass annual condition and operation inspections by your ABS surveyor during periodic/special surveys.

**Additional chemical-cargo SCBA** (if applicable): If your tanker carries cargoes under **ABS MVR Pt.5C2 Ch.9 Sec.14**, additional SCBA sets are required for cargo pump-room entry in gas-filled compartments. Those sets must permit work for at least 20 minutes and include a complete safety ensemble (protective clothing, fireproof lifeline, explosion-proof lamp). This is *in addition to* SOLAS-mandated fire-fighter outfits.

---

## INSPECTION & COMPLIANCE

During USCG Port State Control or ABS survey inspection, expect verification of:
- SCBA quantity per subchapter requirement
- Air cylinder pressure and hydrostatic test dates
- Condition of facepiece, head straps, breathing tubes, hose connections
- Lifeline integrity and snap-hook functionality
- Storage location accessibility and marking
- Crew familiarity with donning and use (drills)

---

## KEY TAKEAWAY

Your vessel must carry NIOSH/MSHA-approved pressure-demand SCBA with 1,200 L air cylinders, two spare charges per unit (or one if you have a dedicated compressor), fireproof lifelines, and full personal protective equipment stored in an accessible, marked location. ABS survey and USCG inspection will verify compliance. If you carry chemical cargoes, additional SCBA sets are required for cargo-space entry.

I've noted these details about your vessel and will remember them for future questions.

query: How many firefighter's outfits does my vessel require?

haiku.answer:
**Your MAERSK Tennessee requires at least two firefighter's outfits.**

For your US-flagged 74,642 GT containership on international routes, the binding requirement is straightforward: (46 CFR 96.35-10(b)) states "Every vessel shall carry at least two firemen's outfits," and this mirrors the international baseline under (SOLAS Ch.II-2 Reg.10.2.1).

---

**What the regulations specify:**

Each outfit must include (46 CFR 96.35-10(a)):
- One self-contained breathing apparatus
- One lifeline with belt or harness
- One flashlight
- One flame safety lamp (or oxygen depletion meter approved by a Coast Guard-recognized independent laboratory)
- One rigid helmet
- Boots and gloves
- Protective clothing
- One fire ax

**No additional outfits required for cargo ships.** The SOLAS provision (10.2.3) that requires *additional* outfits applies only to tankers. Passenger ships require additional outfits based on deck length and main vertical zones, but those do not apply to your containership.

**Spares:** You must also carry at least two spare charges for each breathing apparatus (SOLAS 10.2.5), unless your vessel has an onboard system to recharge air cylinders, in which case one spare per apparatus is acceptable.

---

Your USCG inspection will verify both the number and the condition of the outfits at each Port State Control or vessel examination.

haiku.answer:
For your U.S.-flagged Subchapter T passenger vessel (*Island Explorer*, 65 GT), here's what you must submit for MMC renewal:

## Core Application Package

**Complete CG Form 719B** — signed application with accurate mailing address, contact information, and endorsement(s) you seek. Double-check all details before submitting.

**Proof of TWIC or TWIC application** — (46 CFR 10.227(d)(2)). You must either hold a valid TWIC or provide evidence that you've applied for one.

**Evaluation fee payment receipt** — minimum $50 for renewal of a national (non-officer) rating endorsement, per 46 CFR 10.219. Print your pay.gov receipt and include it with your package. You can pay exam and issuance fees later if needed.

**Drug test compliance** — submit a DOT 5-panel drug test result or employer/consortium letter dated within the past 185 days from your application submission date (46 CFR 10.227(d)(5)). Failure to provide this will return your application.

**Medical certificate** — either hold a currently valid CG-719 medical certificate, or submit a new CG 719K application along with your MMC renewal. For Subchapter T (small passenger vessel), medical requirements are less stringent than STCW-equivalent vessels, but proof of current or pending medical qualification is required (46 CFR 10.227(d)(6)).

**Original or copy of current credential** — if your MMC is still valid, submit a front-and-back photocopy of all pages and attachments. If expired, submit the original (46 CFR 10.227(d)(4)).

**CG Form 719C** — Disclosure Statement for Narcotics, DWI/DUI, and convictions. For renewals, list only convictions NOT previously reported to the Coast Guard. **Failure to report new convictions will delay your credential and may result in denial.**

**Consent to NDR check** — sign the consent form for a Coast Guard National Driver Register check for moving violations (46 CFR 10.227(d)(7)).

---

## Sea Service or Alternative Renewal Requirement

Unless your MMC has been expired more than 6 years, you must meet ONE of these (46 CFR 10.227(e)(1)):

1. **360 days of sea service during the past 5 years** from the date stamped on your application (per MCP-FM-NMC5-01 and 46 CFR 10.227), OR
2. **Pass a comprehensive, open-book exercise** covering general subject matter in 46 CFR Subpart B, OR
3. **Complete an approved refresher training course**, OR
4. **Provide evidence of employment as a qualified instructor** or in a position closely related to vessel operation, construction, or repair.

---

## Timing & Processing

- You may renew **at any time during the MMC's validity and for up to 1 year after expiration** (46 CFR 10.227(b)).
- Submit your complete package to the NMC to meet the 30-day processing goal.
- The NMC Customer Service Center is reachable at 1-888-IASKNMC (427-5662), via email at IASKNMC@uscg.mil, or through the online chat at www.uscg.mil/nmc.

---

**Key reminder:** Missing documentation (especially the drug test or medical certificate) will result in your application being returned. Ensure all forms are complete, signed, and dated before submission.

haiku.answer:
For your U.S.-flag containership **MAERSK Tennessee**, the medical standards for type 2 diabetes are set by the USCG and applied through the National Maritime Center (NMC) when you renew or upgrade your Merchant Mariner Credential (MMC).

## The Core Standard

**Type 2 diabetes controlled by oral medication is waiverable** — meaning you can obtain MMC certification, but you must provide supporting medical documentation. **Type 2 diabetes requiring insulin is treated the same as insulin-dependent diabetes and requires a physical waiver and more rigorous documentation.**

(NVIC 04-08 Ch-2 §4, entries 193–194; USCG MSM 16000.8B Ch.17)

---

## If You Take Oral Medication (non-insulin)

Per **NVIC 04-08 §4 entry 194**, your examining medical practitioner must provide:

- **Internal Medicine consultation** documenting:
  - Interval history, blood pressure, and weight
  - Fasting plasma glucose evaluation
  - **Two current HgA1C tests** (target <8.0), separated by at least 90 days, with the most recent no more than 90 days old
  - **Ophthalmology consultation** (eye exam to screen for diabetic complications)

The 8.0 HgA1C threshold is the ceiling — results above that indicate poor control and trigger denial or waiver review.

---

## If You Require Insulin

Per **NVIC 04-08 §4 entry 193**, the bar is higher:

- **Internal Medicine or Endocrinology consultation** documenting the same elements as above (interval history, blood pressure, weight, fasting glucose, two HgA1C tests <8.0 at least 90 days apart)
- **Graded exercise test** (cardiac stress test) — this is the key additional requirement for insulin-dependent diabetes
- **Ophthalmology consultation**

Additionally, per **USCG MSM 16000.8B Ch.17**, you must provide your physician's written confirmation that:
- You've completed a **comprehensive diabetes education program** (diet, insulin types, storage, blood glucose monitoring, self-adjustment of insulin, recognition of loss of control, effects of illness/stress/exercise)
- **No hospitalizations in the past 12 months**
- Your diabetic control is **stable** (total daily insulin dose has varied less than 10 units up or down)
- You can maintain control by **monitoring blood glucose and adjusting insulin dosage**
- **Copies of medical records for the past 18 months** (at least three entries, demonstrating stable disease)
- **HgbA1C within one month** of your waiver request, ideally within normal limits

---

## Top AI (Additional Information) Triggers

The NMC's **2021 data** shows diabetes is one of the top five reasons for "awaiting information" (AI) letters that delay your application. Common missing pieces:

- Incomplete or outdated HgA1C results (must be within 90 days for oral; within one month preferred for insulin)
- No ophthalmology report
- Insufficient physician documentation of stable control and education history
- Lack of recent medical records (less than three entries in 18 months suggests poor follow-up)

**Pro tip:** Before you submit your MMC application, have your physician compile a summary letter addressing all the elements above. The NMC processes ~50,000 applications annually; incomplete packages routinely receive AI requests that delay approval by weeks or months.

---

## Practical Next Steps

1. **If oral medication:** Schedule an Internal Medicine consultation (not just your primary care doc — the NMC expects a specialist letter) and ophthalmology exam. Request two HgA1C tests 90+ days apart, with the latest within 90 days of application.
2. **If insulin:** Add a graded exercise test (stress test), and ensure your physician's letter covers the 10-point diabetes education and stability checklist (Figure 4-2 in the USCG manual).
3. **Submit complete package:** Include the physician's letter, both HgA1C lab reports, ophthalmology report, medical records summary, and a 12-month hospitalization statement signed by your doctor.

The standard is **waiverable, not disqualifying** — but completeness and timeliness of documentation are what separate fast approvals from multi-month delays.

query: Crossing situation right-of-way if I'm overtaking another vessel?

haiku.answer:
**You have no right-of-way in an overtaking situation — you must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of crossing geometry.**

For your U.S.-flag towing vessel *Mississippi Hauler* operating inland, this is absolute under COLREGs Rule 13 (the Inland Rules version at 33 CFR 83.13).

---

## The Overtaking Rule

**COLREGs Rule 13(a)** states plainly: *"any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken."* This duty is unambiguous — you do not have right-of-way simply because you are crossing the other vessel's course at some point during the overtaking maneuver.

**Rule 13(d)** reinforces this: *"Any subsequent alteration of the bearing between the two vessels shall not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel within the meaning of these Rules or relieve her of the duty of keeping clear of the overtaken vessel until she is finally past and clear."*

In plain English: even if the geometry momentarily looks like a crossing situation (your vessel's bearing relative to the other vessel changes), you remain the give-way vessel and must stay clear until you have completely passed and are fully clear of the overtaken vessel.

---

## Definition of "Overtaking"

You are deemed to be overtaking when you approach another vessel from more than 22.5° abaft her beam — that is, from such a position that at night you would see only her sternlight and neither of her sidelights (Rule 13(b)).

Once you enter the overtaking cone (that 22.5° abaft-beam zone), the overtaking rule applies for the *entire maneuver*. Bearing changes do not convert you to a crossing vessel and do not trigger right-of-way — you remain the give-way vessel until you are past and clear.

---

## Sound Signals in Narrow Channels

For inland operations in narrow channels (Rule 9(e)), your *Mississippi Hauler* must signal your intent to overtake:
- **One short blast** if proposing to overtake on the other vessel's starboard side.
- **Two short blasts** if proposing to overtake on the other vessel's port side.

The vessel being overtaken may agree by sounding the same signal, or refuse by sounding the danger signal (five or more short blasts) if in doubt — but the overtaking rule itself does not change. You remain obligated to keep clear.

---

## Practical Summary

- **Overtaking = give-way, always.** No crossing geometry relieves this.
- **Signal your intention** in narrow channels per Rule 9(e).
- **Remain clear until fully past** — do not assume crossing rules apply mid-maneuver.
- **When in doubt, assume you are overtaking** and act accordingly (Rule 13(c)).

haiku.answer:
**For your U.S.-flagged containership MAERSK Tennessee operating on international routes, you must install and operate a Coast Guard-approved ballast water management system (BWMS) and meet the applicable ballast water discharge standard whenever discharging into U.S. waters.** This is the binding operational requirement under 33 CFR 151.2025(a)(1).

---

## PRIMARY REQUIREMENT: BWMS Installation & Operation

You have three compliant ballast water management methods available under 33 CFR 151.2025(a):

**1. Install and operate a Coast Guard-approved BWMS (the standard path)**
- The BWMS must be approved by the Coast Guard under 46 CFR Part 162.
- Once installed per the compliance schedule in 33 CFR 151.2035(b), you must maintain it in accordance with all manufacturer specifications.
- You must meet the ballast water discharge standard (BWDS) at 33 CFR 151.2030 **at all times of discharge into U.S. waters**.
- Submit any BWMS approval requests to the Coast Guard Marine Safety Center (MSC): msc@uscg.mil or by mail to Stop 7430, 2703 MLK Jr. Avenue SE, Washington DC 20593-7430.

**2. Use only water from a U.S. Public Water System (PWS)**
- The water must come from a U.S. PWS as defined in 40 CFR 141.2 and meet 40 CFR Parts 141 and 143 (drinking water standards).
- You must maintain records showing which PWS supplied the water, plus receipts/invoices from that PWS.
- You must certify that your ballast tanks were either (a) previously cleaned with all residual sediment removed and no subsequent ambient water introduced, OR (b) never had ambient water introduced.
- You may use PWS water exclusively for ballast unless authorized by 33 CFR 151.2040.

**3. Perform complete ballast water exchange (BWE) — if still eligible**
- Exchange must occur in an area **200 nautical miles from any shore** and in waters **more than 2,000 meters deep**.
- This method is only available if your vessel's compliance date has NOT passed per the schedule in 33 CFR 151.2035(b). Once your compliance date passes, BWE is no longer an option unless you are enrolled in the Coast Guard's Supplemental Environmental Project (STEP) program.

---

## ALTERNATIVE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (AMS)

If you installed an Alternative Management System (AMS) prior to your compliance date, you may continue using it for **up to 5 years** from your otherwise-required BWDS compliance date. After that window, you must transition to a Coast Guard-approved BWMS per 33 CFR 151.2025(a)(1).

---

## EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES & EQUIPMENT FAILURE

If your BWMS malfunctions or fails during a voyage, you must report the problem to the Captain of the Port (COTP) as soon as practicable per 33 CFR 151.1515(b). You may continue to the next port of call subject to COTP or USCG Great Lakes District directions.

---

## MANDATORY BEST PRACTICES (33 CFR 151.2050)

Regardless of which management method you use, you must:

- **Avoid** uptake or discharge in marine sanctuaries, preserves, parks, or coral reef areas.
- **Minimize** ballast uptake in areas with harmful algal blooms, near sewage outfalls, dredging operations, poor tidal flushing, or poor visibility.
- **Clean ballast tanks regularly** and dispose of sediments per local/State/Federal regulations.
- **Discharge only the minimal ballast water** essential for vessel operations while in U.S. waters.
- **Rinse anchors and chains** when retrieved to remove organisms at their origin.
- **Remove fouling organisms** from hull, piping, and tanks regularly.
- **Maintain a ballast water management (BWM) plan** specific to your vessel, approved by your company, detailing safety procedures, implementation of mandatory requirements, fouling maintenance, sediment removal, coordination with Coast Guard authorities, designated officer responsibilities, and reporting procedures for U.S. ports you may visit per 33 CFR 151.2050(g).

---

## RECORD-KEEPING & DOCUMENTATION

Maintain ballast water records in your ballast water record book (BWRB) documenting all uptake, discharge, exchange, and treatment activities. This is required under the same CFR sections and supports compliance verification during Coast Guard inspections and Port State Control examinations.

---

## SUMMARY FOR YOUR VESSEL

For international containership operations discharging into U.S. waters: **BWMS installation is the standard, binding compliance path.** The exchange and PWS methods are alternatives if you are still within your compliance window or meet specific conditions; once your compliance date passes, BWMS is mandatory. Invest in a Coast Guard-approved system, maintain it per manufacturer specs, and document all ballast operations.

Every entry must be made in indelible ink, signed by the officer in charge, and the completed page must be signed by the master.** (33 CFR 151.25; MARPOL Annex I Regs. 17 & 36)

---

## Which Operations Require ORB Entries?

**PART I — Machinery Space Operations** (33 CFR 151.25(d)):
- Ballasting or cleaning of fuel oil tanks
- Discharge of ballast containing oily mixture or cleaning water from fuel oil tanks
- Disposal of oil residue
- Discharge or disposal of bilge water from machinery spaces
- Bunkering of fuel or bulk lubricating oil
- Any failure of oil filtering equipment (and reasons)

**PART II — Cargo/Ballast Operations** (33 CFR 151.25(e); MARPOL Annex I Reg. 36):
- Loading of oil cargo
- Internal transfer of oil cargo during voyage
- Unloading of oil cargo
- Ballasting of cargo tanks and dedicated clean ballast tanks
- Cleaning of cargo tanks (including crude oil washing)
- Discharge of ballast except from segregated ballast tanks
- Discharge of water from slop tanks
- Closing of valves after slop tank discharge operations
- Closing of valves for isolation of dedicated clean ballast tanks
- Disposal of oil residue
- **Any failure of the oil discharge monitoring and control system** (MARPOL Annex I Reg. 36.6)
- **Any accidental or exceptional discharge of oil or oily mixture** (statement of circumstances and reasons)

---

## Documentation Requirements

Each entry must include — on a tank-to-tank basis if appropriate:

1. **Date** of the operation
2. **Code (letter)** identifying the item type
3. **Item (number)** corresponding to the specific operation
4. **Full record** of the operation and circumstances
5. **Signature of the officer in charge** of that operation
6. **Master's signature** on the completed page

Per NVIC 08-83 and 33 CFR 151.25(h), entries shall be made **without delay** — as soon as the operation is completed. If unavoidable delay occurs, the entry shall be made at the earliest opportunity. Entries must be in **indelible ink**.

---

## Record Retention & Inspection

- **Retention period**: 3 years after the last entry (33 CFR 151.25(k); MARPOL Annex I Reg. 36.7)
- **Location**: Keep the ORB **readily available for inspection at all reasonable times** and **on board the ship** (33 CFR 151.25(i))
- **Master responsibility**: The master is responsible for the maintenance and accuracy of the ORB (33 CFR 151.25(j))

---

## Form & Electronic Records

The ORB shall follow the form specified in **MARPOL Annex I Appendix III**. An official U.S. Government printed ORB is available from any Coast Guard Sector Office, Marine Inspection Office, or Captain of the Port Office (33 CFR 151.25(b)). You may also use an electronic record book if it is approved by your flag (the U.S. Coast Guard), per MARPOL resolution MEPC.312(74).

If you need a printed ORB form or have specific questions about what to record for a particular operation, contact your local USCG Marine Inspection Office.

Here's the binding requirement:

## Binding U.S. Rule — 46 CFR 199.250

Since your vessel is US-flagged and operates internationally, **46 CFR 199.250** is the controlling regulation. It requires:

- **Weekly** abandon-ship and fire drills (46 CFR 199.250(a))
- **Each crew member** must participate in **at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill each month** (46 CFR 199.250(b))

---

Your vessel also falls under **SOLAS Ch.III Reg.19** (all ships), which establishes the international baseline:

- Every crew member shall participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill **every month** (SOLAS III/19.3.2)
- If more than 25% of your crew have not participated in drills in the previous month, the master must hold both drills within **24 hours of leaving port** (SOLAS III/19.3.2)
- Drills shall be conducted as if there were an actual emergency (SOLAS III/19.3.1)

---

## Practical Summary

**Minimum compliance:**
- Monthly drill participation by each crew member ✓
- Weekly drills as standard practice ✓

**If crew rotation occurs:** If more than 25% of your crew join after drills were last held, you must conduct both drills within 24 hours of departure.

**Lifeboat launch frequency:** Each lifeboat must be launched and maneuvered in the water at least once every **three months** during an abandon ship drill (SOLAS III/19.3.3).

---

The U.S. rule (weekly) is more stringent than the international minimum (monthly), so 46 CFR is your binding floor.

**1. Letter of Warning**

**2. Civil Penalty**
The COTP or OCMI initiates civil penalty proceedings for:
- All major non-criminal violations
- Repeat offenses
- Any minor violation NOT corrected before your next U.S. port call

Penalty amounts are determined by the circumstances, seriousness, culpability, prior violation history, and economic benefit of noncompliance. Civil penalties are adjudicated by Coast Guard hearing officers under 33 CFR 1.07. (USCG MSM 16000.73 Ch.2; USCG MSM 16000.10A Ch.12)

Whenever a civil penalty case is pursued, the PSCO normally requires an LOU or Surety Bond from your vessel's owner, operator, or person in charge to ensure payment of any assessed penalty or fine. (USCG MSM 16000.73 Ch.2)

**4. Detention**
The COTP or OCMI detains your vessel when deficiencies render it **unfit to proceed** without danger to the ship, persons on board, or the marine environment. Detention remains in effect until deficiencies are corrected and the vessel demonstrates it can proceed safely. (USCG MSM 16000.73 Ch.2)

**Your Island Explorer operates under Subchapter T (Uninspected Passenger Vessels) at 65 GT, so you'll need a Restricted Operator of Uninspected Passenger Vessels (ROUPV) endorsement to legally command the vessel.**

Here's the step-by-step process:

## 1. **Determine if Your Waterway Has an Approved Restricted Route**

Before applying, the specific inland waterway where your vessel operates must have a Coast Guard-approved restricted route. This is a prerequisite — you cannot get a ROUPV endorsement for a waterway that hasn't been vetted by your local OCMI (Officer in Charge of Marine Inspection).

- If the route doesn't yet exist, your vessel operator or company must **request approval from the cognizant OCMI** for that geographic area.
- The OCMI conducts a risk assessment of the waterway, evaluating navigational complexity, vessel traffic, waterway characteristics, casualty/incident data, and availability of emergency resources — then approves or denies the restricted route (CG-MMC PL 01-16).

## 2. **Build Your Sea Service**

You must complete **at least 3 months of service operating the same type of vessel on each body of water** for which you request the endorsement (46 CFR 11.467(g)(1)).

Document this service carefully — it will be required on your application.

## 3. **Pass the ROUPV Examination**

The standard ROUPV examination consists of two components:

- **Inland Rules of the Road:** Minimum 50 questions; 80% pass score required.
- **Navigation, Deck General, and Deck Safety:** Minimum 60 questions; 70% pass score required.

Alternatively, you may complete a **Coast Guard-approved OUPV course** in lieu of the standard examination (CG-MMC PL 01-16, 46 CFR 11.467(f)(2)).

## 4. **Meet Medical and Character Requirements**

Submit:
- **CG-719K (Merchant Mariner Medical Certificate)** showing you pass vision, hearing, medical, and physical exams per 46 CFR 10.301.
- **Evidence of passing a drug test** or qualifying for an exemption under 46 CFR 16.220.
- **An official oath** per 46 CFR 10.225(b)(9).
- **Consent to a Coast Guard National Driver Register review** per 46 USC 7101(g).

## 5. **First Aid and CPR Certification**

Obtain current **First Aid and CPR course certificates** (American National Red Cross, American Heart Association, or Coast Guard-approved) per 46 CFR 11.467(a)(4) and 11.201(i). The Coast Guard must determine whether your geographic area's emergency resources are adequate; if not, these are mandatory.

## 6. **Submit Your Application**

Once the restricted route is approved and you've completed your service, pass your exams, and gathered your documents, submit your **application for an MMC with a Restricted OUPV endorsement** to the National Maritime Center (NMC). Your local OCMI office can guide you on the exact application package and form checklist (consult **NMC Application Checklists** for the current checklist).

## Key Takeaway

The process is gated: **your waterway must be approved first** — you cannot apply for a ROUPV endorsement in a vacuum. If your inland route hasn't been approved yet, work with your OCMI to get that approval before investing time in sea service and exam prep. Once the route is live, the sea service, exam, and credential requirements are straightforward.

Contact your cognizant OCMI's credentialing office or the NMC at (202) 372-2357 (MMCpolicy@uscg.mil) to confirm the status of your specific waterway and your next steps.
